Nvidia's former top sales executive has been drawn into fresh questions surrounding an alleged $2.5 billion scheme to divert advanced American AI technology to China, after a short seller highlighted a possible personal connection between him and a former Super Micro Computer official mentioned in a shareholder lawsuit.

Ajay "Jay" Puri, who previously oversaw Nvidia's worldwide sales operations, appeared in photographs with a woman identified as Cenly Chen or Cenly Puri, according to a report published by Muddy Waters Research. The firm questioned whether she was the same Cenly Chen who served as Super Micro's chief growth officer and whose responsibilities have come under scrutiny in litigation involving alleged violations of U.S. export restrictions.

The report does not establish that the woman pictured with Puri is the former Super Micro executive or independently verify a marital relationship. Neither Puri nor Chen has been charged in the federal criminal case, and the allegations involving Chen in the shareholder lawsuit have not been proven.

The questions are significant because Puri was among Nvidia's most senior executives before stepping down from his position in June, while Super Micro is a major customer that uses Nvidia's advanced graphics processors in its AI servers.

The shareholder lawsuit filed against Super Micro in October contains allegations from former employees concerning Chen's role in obtaining and allocating Nvidia chips.

According to the complaint, a former Super Micro sales director alleged that Chen managed the company's acquisition of graphics processors from Nvidia and decided how the limited supply would be distributed among customers.

The former employee also alleged that Chen regularly discussed chip allocations with Super Micro Chief Executive Charles Liang and sought approval for decisions involving major customers.

Another former employee claimed there was no way Chen could have been unaware of the company's alleged improper sales activities.

Those accounts are allegations included in a civil complaint, not findings by a court or conclusions reached by federal prosecutors.

The lawsuit also cites a former employee's allegation that Chen requested the release of Nvidia chips bearing serial numbers associated with products allegedly diverted to China. That claim has not been independently established.

The litigation followed a criminal investigation disclosed in March, when the U.S. Justice Department announced charges against three individuals accused of conspiring to circumvent American export controls.

title: 3 Storage Device Stocks to Buy as the Industry Gains Momentum

3 Storage Device Stocks to Buy as the Industry Gains Momentum
Vaishali Doshi

QMCO

Trading disclosure

Accelerating digital transformation, edge computing, the proliferation of AI workloads and enterprise cloud adoption are driving demand for reliable, scalable and cost-efficient data storage solutions, supporting long-term growth for the Zacks Computer-Storage Devices industry. As hyperscalers double down on AI clusters, companies like Western Digital Corporation WDC are benefiting from robust demand for high-capacity hard disk drives (HDDs) to support the growing storage requirements of AI-driven data centers. HDDs are among the most reliable and economical solutions for mass data storage, forming the backbone of global data infrastructure. Increasing investments in AI infrastructure and data center buildout are expected to sustain demand for enterprise storage solutions.

As cyberattacks continue to increase in frequency, the demand for end-to-end encryption will also drive growth in secure storage solutions. These factors propel the demand for sophisticated data storage solutions, bolstering computer storage product requirements. These factors are favorable for prominent industry players like Western Digital, Super Micro Computer SMCI and Quantum Corporation QMCO. Escalating trade and geopolitical tensions and their impact on supply chains, along with global macroeconomic turbulence and associated inflation, remain headwinds. Rising memory and component prices are also emerging as concerns, potentially affecting customers' spending decisions.

Industry Description

The Zacks Computer-Storage Devices industry houses companies that design, develop, manufacture and market various HDDs and SSDs. These drives are utilized in PCs, laptops, mobiles, servers, network-attached storage devices, video game consoles, digital video recorders and other consumer electronic devices. Some industry participants, including Pure Storage, provide software-defined all-flash solutions that are uniquely fast and cloud-capable for customers. Many industry players offer high-performance modular memory subsystems, mount and blade server systems, enterprise storage and data management software, and hardware products and services. Some industry participants also provide purpose-built servers for storing and accessing data over a shared network or the Internet.

3 Trends Shaping the Computer-Storage Industry's Future

AI's Impact on the Storage Devices Industry: Rapid proliferation of AI is overhauling the entire tech landscape. AI workloads like training large language models and running inference are driving demand for high-speed, high-capacity and low-latency storage solutions. Traditional storage architectures are insufficient for the data throughput required by AI applications, prompting a transition toward NVMe-based SSDs (PCIe Gen 4/5/6), software-defined storage and storage-class memory. Object storage is best suited for storing unstructured data, a common prerequisite for AI workloads. Other fast-emerging solutions include Parallel File Systems Optimized for AI and QLC NAND SSDs for AI Data Lakes. The deployment of AI-optimized servers and the expansion of data centers are driving demand for high-capacity enterprise HDDs and advanced flash storage systems.

Key Takeaways

Dell stock fell 16% in the past week as AI hardware sold off after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO, and Super Micro and CoreWeave fell too.

Steve Eisman warns Dell will slow along with Nvidia, but Cisco just raised its AI forecast and analysts have raised Dell's earnings estimates slightly.

Dell's bigger exposure is the money it lends to customers: its lowest-grade financing receivables more than doubled to $4.4 billion in six months.

Dell trades below its usual forward multiple, but its Nov. 24 report needs to show free cash flow catching up with profits before the stock looks like a buy.

Dell Technologies (DELL:NYSE) is down 16% in the past week, and almost none of the news behind the drop was Dell's own. Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) announced Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO on Nov. 12, and AI hardware sold off with it: Nvidia fell 13%, Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) 20% and CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) 21%.

Steve Eisman, host of The Real Eisman Playbook podcast, thinks the damage will spread. "The picks and shovels companies like Arista, Cisco and Dell will also slow along with NVIDIA, proportionate to the slowdown in data center build out," he said on his Nov. 13 episode. But the day before, Cisco (CSCO:NASDAQ) had raised its forecast for this fiscal year's AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to $9 billion, more than double last year's total.

Dell got pulled into Nvidia's mess

Dell did get one headline of its own. Before the open on Nov. 13, a report traced banned Nvidia H800 chips to a Shanghai data center. Documents showed that Singapore's Aperia Cloud Services had bought 22 Dell servers carrying them. Dell had already cut off Aperia in February 2025, so that's old news. On Nov. 16, Morgan Stanley cut its target to $403 from $511 and Citi cut its target to $550 from $600, and both kept their ratings. A day later, Bernstein held its $650 target. Nvidia's stronger-than-expected report on Nov. 17 lifted Dell before the next day's open, but the gain faded as the broader market fell.

title: What Has The Market Missed In Hewlett Packard Enterprise Stock's Drop?
detail:
What Has The Market Missed In Hewlett Packard Enterprise Stock's Drop?
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) booked record networking orders in fiscal Q3 2026, after buying Juniper Networks. That may be what HPE bulls are betting on. Yet the shares fell 17.5% in the month to November 17, 2026. The S&P 500 fell 4.5% over the same dates. Record orders and a falling share price do not seem to fit together. So how much of that networking demand is HPE turning into sales?

HPE Books Networking Orders Faster Than It Ships

Only part of it, so far. On the September 2, 2026 call, management said orders for its networking gear for AI reached $700 million in fiscal Q3 2026. That was up by triple digits. Cumulative orders for this gear reached $2.2 billion, past the company's target for fiscal 2026. So management raised its year-end target to $2.5 billion to $3 billion.

Sales have moved more slowly. Management said networking orders were growing 3.5 times faster than networking revenue. Networking revenue was $2.9 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, up 10% on management's normalized basis. Management said supply constraints limited how much demand it could turn into revenue. Data center networking revenue fell 6%, which management put down to shipment timing driven by those constraints.

Management expects networking revenue to grow 11% to 13% from a year earlier in fiscal Q4 2026, on order strength and better supply. HPE is shipping more networking gear, just not as fast as customers are ordering it.

Can Networking Hold Up HPE's Margins?

So far, it has. Management said gross margin topped 40% in fiscal Q3 2026 on its own adjusted measure. Disciplined pricing in traditional servers and a larger share of networking helped. Networking earned an operating margin of 22%, against 17% for Cloud & AI, the server and AI systems segment. Both figures are on management's adjusted basis.

HPE expects that difference to last. For fiscal 2027, management's framework puts networking's operating margin in the mid- to high 20% range, against about 13% for Cloud & AI. HPE's networking gear is also part of two recent deals. HPE said on its fiscal Q3 call that Oracle will deploy HPE Juniper routers and switches across one of the largest AI cloud build-outs. On September 30, 2026, HPE announced a $1.2 billion order from Vultr for AMD Helios racks with HPE Networking scale-up switching.

The worry for a holder is one management raised itself. It expects gross margin to move back toward more historical levels as AI systems grow and traditional server pricing normalizes, with more networking offsetting that. It also expects the company's operating margin to fall in fiscal Q4 2026 from fiscal Q3. The main causes are a higher mix of AI systems and pricing.

title: Wife of senior Nvidia executive embroiled in chip smuggling scandal

Jay Puri, an Nvidia executive, and Cenly Chen, who worked at Super Micro

The wife of one of Jensen Huang's most senior allies has been caught up in a chip-smuggling scandal that has engulfed one of Nvidia's biggest partners.

Cenly Chen, who is reportedly married to Jay Puri, an Nvidia executive, worked at Super Micro, a technology company where senior executives have been accused of smuggling $2.5bn (£1.9bn) worth of chips to China.

In a lawsuit brought by shareholders of Super Micro, investors allege there was "no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge about the company's illicit sales". Super Micro has yet to file a response to the claims.

Ms Chen was previously chief growth officer at Super Micro, which packages Nvidia chips into computer servers.

US prosecutors charged some of the company's leading executives earlier this year over involvement in an illicit chip smuggling scheme.

Super Micro has insisted it has co-operated with the US government's investigation and has not been named in its indictment. Ms Chen is not named in the US charges.

However, the revelations come amid mounting scrutiny on Nvidia's ties to the Far East over claims Mr Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Muddy waters, a short-selling firm, raised questions over Ms Chen's ties to Nvidia on Tuesday night.

The firm noted how Ms Chen had been repeatedly photographed alongside Mr Puri and named in photographs as Cenly Puri.

The pair are reportedly married, technology news site The Information reported on Wednesday.

Nvidia has already been the subject of intense pressure over claims that Chinese companies sought to access its chips through illegal smuggling and legal loopholes.

Nvidia's graphics chips are widely used to develop powerful AI technology.

The Super Micro scandal, which emerged earlier this year, saw Wally Liaw, the company's co-founder, charged by the US government for allegedly diverting advanced Nvidia chips via Taiwan to customers in China.

Mr Liaw has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Mr Huang resigned last Thursday over claims he had a relationship with Alice Huang, who worked at another Nvidia customer, Megaspeed.

Megaspeed, based in Singapore, has also been investigated by the US for smuggling over claims it diverted powerful Nvidia chips to China. The company has denied wrongdoing.

Nvidia's board rejected an attempt by Mr Huang to return to the company on Tuesday, insisting it had no plans to reinstate him.

The fallout has also triggered scrutiny in the White House.

It emerged on Wednesday that leading Democrats in the US House of Representatives have launched an investigation into whether Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, had used his position to help Cantor Fitzgerald avoid losses from the Nvidia scandal.
